newsitem.title: UK: Euro Crude Outlook - Waits for Iraq to tip scales.
newsitem.headline: Euro Crude Outlook - Waits for Iraq to tip scales.

text.p: In the absence of Iraqi barrels, European crude markets will remain balanced to tight this week, but fresh news about the timing of the resumption of Iraqi exports could quickly swing sentiment, traders said.
"If we have another week without any news then we'll have a confused and uncertain market," said one
"(Iraq) is always in the back of the mind and I don't think people are going to take out big positions until they have a clearer idea of what's going to happen," he added.
Manipulation of the physical market to lift profits on swaps positions could further cloud the picture, traders said.
Benchmark North Sea Dated Brent made steady gains last week to a peak of August Brent +17 cents on Friday, before slumping to trade at August Brent parity late that day.

Traders said that last week's gains were an attempt by a French and a U.S. refiner to push up the market to lift profits on long swaps positions. The sharp fall was an attempt by a British major to bring the price of Dated Brent to a level more conducive with its forward positions, they said.
"They (the major) wanted to bring Dated down next week but they'll have a hard job because there are a lot of companies out there long," said one trader on Friday.
On the fundamental side, expectations that Iraqi flows will not resume at least until mid-August encouraged brisk buying of first and second decade August North Sea grades last week.
But after that wave of short-covering buyers look to be fairly relaxed this week, traders said.
"We've seen a lot of short-covering into the second decade, but it looks like the market has peaked...buyers are relaxed and sellers are not that aggressive," said a North Sea dealer.
Traders reported the same story in the Mediterranean sour market, where refiners have keenly bought up all of the first decade August Urals programme.
At least two early August Syrian Light spot cargoes have also been snapped up.
Urals climbed to Dated Brent -65 cents last week but traders said further gains were unlikely with poor profit margins pushing at least one major refiner in the region to cut runs.
"I don't know whether it'll go any higher, but it's still a tight market. We've got no real signs of Iraqi barrels," said a Mediterranean refiner.
The U.N. said last week that it expected to complete by the end of the month a review of an Iraqi aid plan - which Iraq insists is finalised before it resumes exports.

Traders expect wrangling over new price formulae and the signing of sales contracts to take a further two weeks before oil flows under the third three-month term of the oil-for-food agreement can begin.

The West African crude market, already nearly sold out for August, was given an extra fillip on Friday by a Dubai market rally, narrowing the Brent/Dubai spread and making Nigerian and other grades more attractive to Far East buyers. Less than 500,000 barrel per day of August loadings were bought by Asian refiners in August, half down from July, but a widening arbitrage could see September sales brisker.
